newsitem.title: USA: Mortgage rates fall for 7th consecutive week.
newsitem.headline: Mortgage rates fall for 7th consecutive week.

text.p: Fixed-rate mortgage rates fell for a seventh week in a row as fresh economic data suggested steady economic growth with little risk of inflation, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said Thursday.

Thirty-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 7.44 percent in the week ending Dec. 6, down from 7.52 percent a week ago. The rate has not been lower since the week ended March 8, when the average was 7.38 percent.
Fifteen-year loans fell to 6.96 percent, the lowest since a rate of 6.87 percent in the March 8 week. Last week's rate averaged 7.04 percent.
Adjustable mortgage rates inched down to 5.47 percent from 5.50 percent last week. The rate has not been lower since it stood at 5.40 percent in the March 8 week, Freddie Mac said.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.18 percent, the 15-year 6.74 percent, and the adjustable loan 5.53 percent.
"Interest rates today rival those of the early 1970s," Robert Van Order, Freddie Mac chief economist, said.
"Economic signs of little or no inflation, coupled with a steady, sustainable rate of growth have encouraged the decline in interest rates that we have seen over the last seven weeks."

On Tuesday, the Conference Board said U.S. October leading indicators rose 0.1 percent, while the Commerce Department said sales of U.S. October single-family homes fell 8.7 percent to a 714,000-unit annualized rate.
On Friday, the Labour Department will issue U.S. employment data for November.

Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average of 1.7 percent in fees and points on 30-year loans, down from 1.8 percent last week. They charged 1.7 percent on 15-year loans, unchanged from the previous week, and 1.3 percent on adjustable loans, down from 1.4 percent last week.
